exercises.title: A first observation
exercises.context: stdout!(value) prints a value. Make this program print the Boolean value true. The surrounding new block connects stdout to the built-in output channel.
hints: A Boolean literal is written without quotation marks.
The two Boolean literals are true and false.

exercises.title: An integer is a value
exercises.context: Make the output be the integer 42. An integer literal is a whole number written directly in the program.
hints: Numbers do not need quotation marks.
Use a whole-number literal here.

exercises.title: Words need quotation marks
exercises.context: Print the string hello. Strings use double quotation marks; an unquoted word is treated as an identifier.
hints: The quote characters are part of the source syntax.
Compare the number 42 with the string "42".

exercises.title: Observe a calculation
exercises.context: Make the program print 5. The interpreter evaluates the arithmetic expression before sending its result to stdout.
hints: The + operator adds two integers.
Find the missing addend in 2 + ? = 5.

exercises.title: Ask whether values agree
exercises.context: Make this comparison print true. == compares two values and produces a Boolean.
hints: Both sides of == must have the same value for this test to pass.
An arithmetic expression can stand wherever an integer value is expected.

exercises.title: There can be many right answers
exercises.context: Make the comparison print true. != asks whether two values differ. More than one answer can satisfy this koan.
hints: Choose an integer that differs from 3.
The runner checks the result, so it accepts more than the reference answer.

exercises.title: Parentheses change the calculation
exercises.context: Make this expression produce 21. Parentheses group a subexpression before multiplication.
hints: Work backwards from 21 divided by 3.
The parenthesized sum needs to be 7.

exercises.title: Join two strings
exercises.context: Produce the string firefly. ++ concatenates strings without inserting spaces.
hints: The missing piece is another string.
The result must contain fire immediately followed by fly.

exercises.title: Count from zero
exercises.context: Print 20 from this list. nth selects an element by its zero-based index; the first element has index 0.
hints: Find the index of the second element.
The valid indexes of this list are 0, 1, and 2.

exercises.title: Look up a named value
exercises.context: Print 7 by looking up the right key. A map stores values under keys; get retrieves the value associated with a key.
hints: Map keys are values too; these keys are strings.
Choose the key whose value is 7.

exercises.title: Adding to an immutable set
exercises.context: Make the new set have three elements. Sets hold unique values; add returns a new set and size counts its members.
hints: Adding an existing element does not increase the size.
Choose a value absent from Set(1, 2).

exercises.title: Numeric types must agree
exercises.context: Make this equality true. The suffix n denotes an arbitrary-precision integer. Both operands of + must have the same numeric type.
hints: The missing value must also carry the n suffix.
Ordinary 25 and arbitrary-precision 25n are different numeric types.

exercises.title: Address the message
exercises.context: Send 7 to inbox. The receive below waits for a message on inbox, binds its value as n, and prints it.
hints: A send is written channel!(message).
Use the name introduced by new, without quotes.

exercises.title: Two processes can run together
exercises.context: Run both sends. The parallel composition operator allows both processes to run; their printed order is not specified.
hints: Use the operator that looks like a vertical bar.
The runner compares these two observations without imposing an order.

exercises.title: Fresh names are distinct
exercises.context: Make the comparison false by comparing two different fresh names. new creates distinct names; * exposes a name as a process value so it can be compared.
hints: left and right are created independently.
Fill in the name different from left; the * is already supplied.

exercises.title: A receiver chooses a channel
exercises.context: Print only 2. Messages on one channel cannot satisfy a receive on a different fresh channel.
hints: Follow the channel that was sent 2.
The unconsumed message on the other channel does not print itself.

exercises.title: A quoted value can name a channel
exercises.context: Receive the message sent on the name made by quoting the string score. @ turns a process value into a name; equal quoted values identify the same channel.
hints: The @ is already present on the receiving side.
The sender quotes a string; use the same string for the receiver.

exercises.title: Doing nothing is a process
exercises.context: Print 7 without adding another action. Nil is the inactive process; composing it in parallel with an action leaves that action alone.
hints: The inactive process starts with a capital N.
The language spelling is Nil.

exercises.title: Use the received value
exercises.context: The @value pattern binds the received process value. Print the value carried by the message, using the binding rather than a new literal.
hints: The name of the binding appears immediately after @.
Inside the receive body, value refers to the received integer.

exercises.title: A name binding needs dereferencing
exercises.context: A receive pattern without @ binds a name quoting the payload. Dereference that name to print the original integer.
hints: * converts a name back into the process it quotes.
Use *value in the body.

exercises.title: Send a process and then run it
exercises.context: Send a process that prints 9. The receiver binds a name for that process, and *code runs it. Processes can be communicated as data.
hints: The missing payload can itself be a send.
The body *code dereferences the received name and activates the quoted process.

exercises.title: Send a reply channel
exercises.context: The request carries a value and a reply channel. The receiver uses ret to send the incremented result back; make the final answer 6.
hints: The second request argument is *reply, so the name pattern ret can use it as a channel.
The arithmetic in the server should add one.

exercises.title: One payload can have structure
exercises.context: A tuple is one message argument containing multiple values. The tuple pattern binds x and y. Print their sum.
hints: The send has one tuple argument, unlike request!(5, *reply).
Choose the integer addition operator.

exercises.title: The number of message arguments matters
exercises.context: Send two separate integer arguments whose sum is 7. The receiver expects two arguments; a single tuple would have the wrong shape.
hints: Separate two message arguments with a comma.
For example, choose integers 3 and 4 as separate arguments.

exercises.title: Match an exact value
exercises.context: Choose the zero branch. match tries patterns in source order; a literal pattern accepts only that value.
hints: Supply a value matching the first pattern.
The underscore in the second branch is a wildcard, not a blank to edit.

exercises.title: Take a tuple apart
exercises.context: The tuple pattern binds each position. Print the sum of the two bound values.
hints: Patterns name parts of the existing value.
x and y are the integers 2 and 3 inside the branch.

exercises.title: Bind the rest of a list
exercises.context: head binds the first element; ...tail binds the remaining list. Print the number of elements in the tail.
hints: The list method length() counts elements.
tail is [3, 5], not the last element alone.

exercises.title: A wildcard supplies a fallback
exercises.context: Make the fallback print other. _ matches any value without creating a binding. This fallback handles 99 after the zero pattern fails.
hints: The missing expression is the output string.
Use a string literal; the wildcard has no value you can refer to.

exercises.title: A pattern can require an integer
exercises.context: Make the integer branch print 42. x /\ Int binds a value only when it has the ordinary integer type.
hints: The branch adds one to the input.
A quoted number is a string and would choose the fallback.

exercises.title: Choose with a Boolean expression
exercises.context: Make the program print yes. if requires a Boolean condition; integers are not automatically treated as true or false.
hints: A comparison produces a Boolean.
For example, compare two ordered integers with <.

exercises.title: A receiver that stays available
exercises.context: Process both messages and print 2 and 3. A persistent receive stays available for subsequent matching messages.
hints: The persistent receive arrow is <=; the one-shot arrow is <-.
There are two messages, so a one-shot receive can only print one result.

exercises.title: A contract is a persistent service
exercises.context: Complete the double service so the reply is 6. contract declares a persistent receiver on a named channel.
hints: The request supplies an integer and a reply channel.
Multiply the integer by 2 before replying.

exercises.title: Serve independent requests
exercises.context: Make the service respond with 11 and 21. Both requests use the same contract, which remains available after the first call.
hints: The requests contain 10 and 20.
Each response should add the same increment.

exercises.title: Recursion needs progress
exercises.context: Print 3, 2, and 1 and stop recursing at zero. The printed order is deliberately not asserted: the print and recursive call run in parallel.
hints: Each recursive call must move toward the stopping condition.
Pass n - 1 to the next call.

exercises.title: Combine a recursive result
exercises.context: Sum a list by asking for the tail sum on a private reply channel, then combining it with the head. The empty list contributes zero.
hints: The result s is the sum of the remaining elements.
Combine h and s with addition.

exercises.title: A service can create another service
exercises.context: The factory creates a private adder that remembers amount. Use the returned adder to produce 12 when amount is 5.
hints: The name returned on made is a channel for the new service.
Choose the input that becomes 12 after adding 5.

exercises.title: Wait for both channels together
exercises.context: Join the two receives so the body runs after one message from each channel is available. The two messages are consumed together.
hints: The join separator is &.
A join differs from |, which composes whole processes.

exercises.title: A later receive can use an earlier binding
exercises.context: First receive a channel name, then receive its message. A semicolon separates sequential receipt groups and makes the first binding available to the second.
hints: The second channel is not known until the first receive completes.
Use ; between these receipt groups.

exercises.title: Read without consuming
exercises.context: Read the same 5 twice and print 10. The first receive must leave the message available for the nested consuming receive.
hints: The peek arrow is <<-.
If the first receive consumes the message, the nested receive has nothing to read.

exercises.title: Replace the state message
exercises.context: A mutable cell is a channel holding the current value. Consume the old value and send an updated one so the final read yields 15.
hints: The current value is 10.
The completion signal gates the final read; it is a separate message carrying Nil.

exercises.title: Order visible actions with an acknowledgment
exercises.context: Print first and then second in that order. stdoutAck signals ack after printing; the receive then enables the second print.
hints: Complete the second output string.
An acknowledgment establishes ordering that two parallel stdout sends do not.

exercises.title: Two updates share a cell
exercises.context: Both increment requests must take the cell value before replacing it. After both acknowledgments, compare the final count with the number of updates.
hints: Only one update can hold the cell message at a time.
There are two increment requests, starting from zero.

exercises.title: A guard filters candidate messages
exercises.context: Accept the positive integer 7. The where condition must be true before the candidate message is consumed.
hints: Choose a comparison that accepts a positive number.
The condition should mean x is greater than zero.

exercises.title: A failed guard leaves the message available
exercises.context: The positive receiver cannot consume -3. The negative receiver can still take that message; print its bound value.
hints: The matching negative receiver binds the integer as x.
A rejected candidate is still available to a different matching receive.

exercises.title: A join guard can compare both messages
exercises.context: Allow the join only when the value from left is smaller than the value from right. The guard sees bindings from both channels.
hints: Write a Boolean comparison using x and y.
Both messages are available, but the guard must also succeed.

exercises.title: A false match guard tries the next case
exercises.context: Print small. The first pattern binds 4, but its guard should reject values at most 10 so matching continues to the fallback.
hints: Matching the pattern alone does not select a guarded case.
Use x > 10 for the first guard.

exercises.title: Each sequential receipt group has a guard
exercises.context: Require a positive value in each receipt group. Each guard checks its own binding; the final body can use both received values.
hints: Compare y against zero in its own group.
The body adds x and y after both guards have passed.

exercises.title: Select a job by its contents
exercises.context: Print job ID 2. Each job is a tuple of ID and score, sent on its own channel. Use the same score threshold in both blanks to reject job 1 and accept job 2.
hints: The scores are 2 and 8.
Any integer threshold greater than 2 and at most 8 satisfies the condition.

exercises.title: Declare a category
exercises.context: A Module packages theory declarations. Types declares the categories of a little language. Complete the category name so the presentation contains Value.
hints: This is a declaration checked by the elaborator, not an executed .rho program.
The final lowercase theory expression chooses which theory to elaborate.

exercises.title: Give a category one term
exercises.context: Terms declares syntax. A rule has a label, an argument context, concrete syntax, and a result category. Complete the category of the constant Zero.
hints: An empty context before |- means this term takes no arguments.
The result category must have been declared by Types.

exercises.title: Choose the theory to elaborate
exercises.context: A module can declare several theories. Select Warm as the entry theory so the resulting presentation contains Color and Red.
hints: The lowercase theory expression is the entry point.
Theory names are followed by parentheses even when no arguments are needed.

exercises.title: Reference a term argument
exercises.context: An argument context gives names and categories to inputs. Use the declared argument exactly once in the concrete syntax of Wrap.
hints: The context before |- declares x:Value.
A quoted "x" is a literal character, whereas unquoted x refers to the argument.

exercises.title: A term with two arguments
exercises.context: Declare the result category of Pair. Both arguments have category Value, and both are referenced in its concrete syntax.
hints: The same declared category can be used for arguments and results.
The presentation should contain a Pair constructor returning Value.

Terms: Pair . left:Value, right:Value |- "(" left "," right ")" : Value;

exercises.title: Labels identify constructors
exercises.context: Add the label One for the second constructor. Labels must be unique within the resulting theory; concrete spellings and labels have different roles.
hints: The constructor label occurs before the dot.
Zero already names the first constructor.

exercises.title: An equation states an identity
exercises.context: Complete the right identity equation for Add. Equations use constructor labels in prefix form; this declares a law rather than performing an addition.
hints: The identity says adding Zero leaves x unchanged.
A nullary constructor is written (Zero) inside an equation.

Terms: Add . x:Value, y:Value |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Value;

exercises.title: Describe commutativity
exercises.context: Declare that swapping the arguments of Add preserves its meaning. Use the constructor label Add in the right-hand expression.
hints: Equations describe an equality between two term shapes.
Exchange x and y in the right-hand Add application.

Terms: Add . x:Value, y:Value |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Value;

exercises.title: A rewrite has a direction
exercises.context: Complete the simplifying rewrite DropZero. ~> describes a directed rule, unlike the symmetric == of an equation.
hints: Removing addition by Zero should leave x.
The elaborator checks and retains this rule; it does not execute a generated evaluator.

Terms: Add . x:Value, y:Value |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Value;

exercises.title: Declare constructors before using them
exercises.context: Choose the already declared constructor Zero in this equation. Builder blocks are processed in order; a rule cannot refer forward to a later constructor.
hints: Look at the Terms block before Equations.
The equation must refer to (Zero), not an undeclared constructor.

Terms: Add . x:Value, y:Value |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Value;

exercises.title: Give each rewrite a name
exercises.context: Name this simplifying rule DropZero. A rewrite name lets tools identify the rule as part of the theory presentation.
hints: The name appears before the colon, not inside the term expression.
Use the requested identifier with its capital letters.

Terms: Add . x:Value, y:Value |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Value;

exercises.title: Keep equations and rewrites distinct
exercises.context: Keep the commutativity equation and complete the directed simplification rule. Both belong to the theory, but they express different relationships.
hints: The equation exchanges arguments; the rewrite removes Zero.
The right-hand side of the simplification is x.

Terms: Add . x:Value, y:Value |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Value;

exercises.title: Extend a supplied theory
exercises.context: A theory parameter supplies an existing presentation. Complete the base of Decorated with its parameter so Value is available when Wrap is added.
hints: The parameter is named b and has theory type Base.
Use b as the body base rather than constructing an unrelated Base().

exercises.title: Rename an exported category
exercises.context: Rename Value to Expr on export. The elaborator carries the category rename into the constructor result as well.
hints: The export arrow maps the existing category to its public spelling.
Use Expr as the new name.

exercises.title: Replace a constructor spelling and label
exercises.context: Replace Zero with Nothing, keeping the category Value. Replacements adapt inherited syntax rather than adding a second constructor.
hints: The target of the replacement is the existing label Zero.
The new label must be Nothing; its concrete spelling is already supplied.

exercises.title: A replacement updates inherited laws
exercises.context: Rename Zero to Nothing. The inherited identity equation must then mention Nothing as well; the elaborator performs that propagation.
hints: Only the constructor replacement belongs in the blank.
The resulting equation should be (Add x (Nothing)) == x.

Terms: Add . x:Value, y:Value |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Value;

exercises.title: Import a module under an alias
exercises.context: Import the bundled local module as lib and choose its Base theory. Imports in this course use local files so the lessons work offline.
hints: The alias prefixes the imported theory name with a dot.
The imported file defines Base with no parameters.

exercises.title: Import one theory by name
exercises.context: Complete the name of the theory imported from the local support module. This import makes Base available without an alias prefix.
hints: The library declares a theory called Base.
The entry expression already calls Base().

exercises.title: Create the common ancestor once
exercises.context: Both extensions must share the same Base instance. Pass the existing b to Right so the join has one category Value.
hints: Calling Base() again would invent another category with the same spelling.
Sharing is established by passing the same bound instance.

exercises.title: Join extensions over their shared base
exercises.context: Combine both extensions so the result contains A and B with a single shared Value category. The theory join operator is written backslash-slash.
hints: The join spelling is \/, distinct from process parallel composition |.
Both arguments already descend from the same b.

exercises.title: Keep the shared fragment
exercises.context: Keep only what Left and Right inherit in common. Their shared ancestor contributes Value; A and B are independent additions.
hints: The meet operator is /\.
The resulting presentation should have Value and no constructors.

exercises.title: A shared constructor appears once
exercises.context: Both branches inherit the same Seed presentation. Pass the existing s to BranchB so joining the branches retains one Zero constructor.
hints: Create Seed(b) once, then share its result with both branches.
A second call to Seed(b) creates a distinct constructor origin.

exercises.title: Subtract by shared origin
exercises.context: Remove the inherited One constructor using the same Mon instance m. Difference removes shared origins, including categories; the final join restores the shared base b so Extra still has its Value category.
hints: The difference operator is a single backslash.
Subtract the previously bound instance m.

exercises.title: Assemble a tiny expression language
exercises.context: Combine values and addition over a shared category, then add a simplification rule. Complete the join and the rewrite result to describe the requested language.
hints: Use the theory join to retain constructors from both branches.
The simplification rule returns x; these declarations describe a language but do not run its expressions.

Terms: Add . x:Expr, y:Expr |- "(" x "+" y ")" : Expr;
